english: don't worry (about me); no need to worry
use: A polite way to turn down someone's concern or offer of help, often with people you don't know well.

example.romaji: hitori de kaeremasu kara, goshinpai naku.
example.ja: 一人で帰れますから、ご心配なく。
example.english: I can get home on my own, so don't worry.

notes: It can sound a bit cool, like I've got this; shinpai shinaide is warmer.

english: go for it!; you can do it!
use: Called out to cheer someone on in sport or before a challenge.

example.ja: 明日試験でしょ？ファイト！
example.english: Your exam's tomorrow, right? You've got this!

notes: From English fight, but it means keep going. Ganbatte is the everyday word.

use: Said to show you understand someone's frustration or sadness, often with yo.

example.romaji: sore wa kuyashii yo ne. kimochi wakaru.
example.ja: それは悔しいよね。気持ちわかる。
example.english: That's so frustrating. I know how you feel.

examplePolite.ja: その気持ち、よくわかります。
examplePolite.english: I really understand how you feel.

notes: Wakaru wakaru is a quick, casual I get it.

use: Said to someone sick or hurt as you part; clinic and pharmacy staff say it as you leave, and you answer arigatou gozaimasu.

example.romaji: kaze hiita no? odaiji ni ne.
example.ja: 風邪ひいたの？お大事にね。
example.english: You caught a cold? Get well soon.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze desu ka? douzo odaiji ni.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪ですか？どうぞお大事に。

notes: Only for illness or injury, not a general goodbye.

politeJa: 無理しないでください
english: don't overdo it; don't push yourself
use: Said to someone sick, tired or overworking; also to let someone off an invitation.

example.romaji: netsu aru n desho? muri shinaide ne.
example.ja: 熱あるんでしょ？無理しないでね。
example.english: You've got a fever, right? Don't push yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii to omoimasu ga, muri shinaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 忙しいと思いますが、無理しないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: I know you're busy, but please don't overdo it.

notes: Muri means too much or impossible; muri! on its own means no way!

english: you did really well; great effort
use: Praise after someone finishes something hard, win or lose; often to kids or juniors.

example.romaji: shiai, oshikatta kedo yoku ganbatta ne.
example.ja: 試合、惜しかったけどよく頑張ったね。
example.english: The game was close, but you did really well.

examplePolite.ja: 長い間、よく頑張りましたね。
examplePolite.english: You worked so hard for so long.

notes: It praises effort, not results. To a superior, otsukaresama deshita is safer.

polite: okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai
politeJa: お体に気をつけてください
english: look after yourself; take care of your health
use: Said at a goodbye before a long gap, or to someone busy or getting older; also ends letters.

example.romaji: samuku natta kara, karada ni ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: 寒くなったから、体に気をつけてね。
example.english: It's gotten cold, so look after yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii jiki desu ga, okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 忙しい時期ですが、お体に気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: It's a busy time, but please take care of yourself.

notes: Ki o tsukete alone means be careful, or take care as a goodbye.

politeJa: ゆっくり休んでください
use: Said to someone sick, tired, or done with a hard stretch of work.

example.romaji: kyou wa hayaku nete, yukkuri yasunde ne.
example.ja: 今日は早く寝て、ゆっくり休んでね。
example.english: Go to bed early tonight and get some good rest.

examplePolite.romaji: konshuu wa taihen deshita ne. yukkuri yasunde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今週は大変でしたね。ゆっくり休んでください。
examplePolite.english: This week was tough. Please get some good rest.

notes: Yasumu means rest, and also take a day off.

politeJa: 元気を出してください
use: Said to someone sad or discouraged, often after a failure or a breakup.

example.romaji: sonna ni ochikomanaide. genki dashite yo.
example.ja: そんなに落ち込まないで。元気出してよ。
example.english: Don't be so down. Cheer up.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi ga arimasu yo. genki o dashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次がありますよ。元気を出してください。
examplePolite.english: There's always next time. Please cheer up.

notes: Genki here means energy or spirits; genki nai ne means you seem down.

politeJa: ゆっくりでいいですよ
use: Said to someone hurrying for your sake; people often say it when you're searching for words.

example.romaji: isoganakute ii kara, yukkuri de ii yo.
example.ja: 急がなくていいから、ゆっくりでいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to hurry. Take your time.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo, yukkuri de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ、ゆっくりでいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's all right, take your time.

notes: To ask someone to slow down: mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai.
